*   **Limitations:** Assumes smooth or periodic motion; may struggle with abrupt, non-periodic changes without high-frequency terms [S2].

The claim states that the method assumes smooth or periodic motion and may struggle with abrupt, non-periodic changes without high-frequency terms. The evidence explicitly states that Katsumata et al. use Fourier series 'inspired by the fact that the motion of human and articulated objects is sometimes periodic' and that 'polynomial fitting and Fourier approximation have advantages in modeling smooth motion'. While the evidence mentions that Gaussian-Flow combines methods to capture residuals (implying handling of more complex motion), the core limitation described in the claim regarding the reliance on periodic/smooth assumptions for the base Fourier/linear approach is directly supported by the text describing the inspiration and advantages of these specific techniques.

Non-periodic motions may require higher $K$ or hybrid models [S2].

The claim states that non-periodic motions may require higher K or hybrid models. The evidence explicitly mentions that Fourier approximation (used for periodic motion) has advantages in modeling smooth motion, while polynomial fitting has advantages in modeling violent motion. It then states that Gaussian-Flow combines these two methods (a hybrid approach) to capture time-dependent residuals. This supports the idea that for motions that are not purely periodic (like violent motion), a hybrid model or more complex modeling (implied by the combination of methods) is required.

Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting models dynamic scenes by keeping Gaussian properties (scale, opacity, spherical harmonics) unchanged over time while parameterizing position and orientation as continuous functions of time [S1, S2].

The claim states that Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting models dynamic scenes by keeping Gaussian properties (scale, opacity, spherical harmonics) unchanged over time while parameterizing position and orientation as continuous functions of time. Source [S1] explicitly states that Luiten et al. introduced dynamic 3D Gaussians to model dynamic scenes by 'keeping the properties of 3D Gaussians unchanged over time while allowing their positions and orientations to change.' Source [S2] corroborates this by describing an explicit deformation method where 'Other attributes remain unchanged over time' and specifies that 'The position, rotation... are considered to change over time' via 'parametric functions... [that] are continuous functions about time.' Since the evidence confirms that properties (other than position and orientation) are unchanged and position/orientation are modeled as continuous functions of time, the claim is fully supported.
